claims.text: The as-manufactured high-entropy alloy is initially a single-phase solid solution.
Service-relevant mechanical loading drives dynamic phase separation in the initially single-phase alloy.
Stress-driven phase separation produces localized precipitates or ordered regions.
The localized precipitates or ordered regions nucleate brittle secondary phases.
Formation of brittle secondary phases reduces alloy toughness.
Formation of brittle secondary phases promotes brittle fracture.
Under the proposed service conditions, diffusion is modest but sufficient for stress-assisted local compositional fluctuations.
The proposed loading temperatures are below those that would independently cause thermal phase transformations.
Nanoscale precipitates or ordered clusters form preferentially at grain boundaries or within grains and act as embrittlement sites.
Mechanical loading accelerates local atomic diffusion in the metastable single-phase alloy.
Mechanical loading accelerates local compositional clustering in the metastable single-phase alloy.
Compositional clusters evolve into brittle secondary phases.
Brittle secondary phases undermine the alloy's ductile, energy-absorbing mechanisms and cause premature crack initiation.
Mechanically loaded samples will have lower fracture toughness and ductility than untreated baseline samples.
Mechanically loaded samples will exhibit emerging nanoscale precipitates or ordered regions that are absent or less prevalent in baseline samples.
The proposed mechanism applies to cyclic or high-strain-rate loading from room to moderately elevated temperatures.
At very high temperatures, thermal diffusion dominates over the proposed stress-driven mechanism.
At very low strains, the proposed stress-driven phase-separation mechanism may not operate.
